Kaldra 0.1.0-preview.1 — render-graph engine for .NET
Generated: 2026-11-23
Source: https://github.com/AtomicBlom/Kaldra

# Kaldra Architecture

Kaldra is a **declarative, render-graph-driven rendering engine for .NET**. You describe *what* each pass reads and writes; the engine derives execution order, GPU barriers, image-layout transitions, transient-resource aliasing, and CPU↔GPU synchronisation.

## Three layers

```
BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core  ──(Describe)──►  BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph  ──(Execute)──►  BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.Vulkan
(your code)                                              BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.DirectX12
```

### Describe — `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core`

Immutable, hashable, fluent builders. You call `RenderGraph.Define` once per structural change and get back an immutable `RenderGraph` value that encodes your full intent:

- `GraphBuilder` — the root builder (`g => { … }`)
- `Domain` — a named resolution domain (fixed size or backbuffer-relative)
- `ColorHandle / DepthHandle / BufferHandle` — typed resource handles
- `PassBuilder` — one GPU pass; declares `.Writes`, `.Blends`, `.Samples`, `.WritesDepth`, `.ReadsDepth`, `.ReadsVertex`, `.ReadWrites`, `.Reads`
- `ConstantsHandle` / `StorageBufferHandle` — neutral per-frame channels the app fills by handle (`IEngine.Write`) and a pass `.Reads`; how view/light/time data reaches a pass without the engine naming a game concept
- Pass callbacks (`.Draw`, `.Dispatch`) — closures that pull per-frame data from `IRenderContext` and from the `Constants`/`Storage` buffers the pass reads, rather than capturing it

No graphics-API type appears here. This layer allocates freely and is safe to call from any thread.

### Execute — `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph`

Per-frame: topological sort from the read/write edges, barrier/layout-transition derivation, transient-resource aliasing, lifetime analysis. Produces backend-neutral scheduling decisions. Both backends consume the same schedule.

`EngineBase` owns the shared engine lifecycle: technique registration, shader hot-reload, GPU-timing decode, and frame capture. Backend-specific execution (command recording) stays in each backend.

### Bake + Record — `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.Vulkan` / `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.DirectX12`

Translate the neutral schedule into real GPU work. Backends:

- Create pipelines and descriptor layouts from the Slang reflection JSON (cached by hash for the engine's lifetime)
- Emit `vkCmdPipelineBarrier2` (Vulkan 1.3) or D3D12 resource transitions
- Call into your pass `.Draw` / `.Dispatch` closures to record draw calls

No graphics-API type leaks into `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core` or `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph`. Introducing one is the cardinal architectural violation.

## Dependency direction

```
                       ┌──► BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.Vulkan    ─┐
your app ──► host ─────┼──► BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.DirectX12 ─┼──► BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph ──► BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core
             │         └──► BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.WebGPU    ─┘
             │
             └── BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Hosting.Desktop (window, surface, frame loop, CLI flags)
                 BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Hosting.Web     (browser, paired with the WebGPU backend)
```

Beside the engine tiers, all backend-neutral and free of graphics-API references:

| Project | Role |
|---|---|
| `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Assets` | image + glTF loaders, and the material upload bridge |
| `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Concepts` | app-side helpers — `Camera`, `Frustum`, `Scene`. Deliberately **not** engine API |
| `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Input` | actions, bindings, layered event routing |
| `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.Vysara` / `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.ImGui` | UI bridges; both reach the GPU only through the neutral draw-list verb, so no backend references a UI library |

In the browser, the host (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.WebGPU/wwwroot/kaldra-webgpu.js`) keeps from the browser the keys it would also act
on but which mean nothing to an app being played in its canvas: F1, F3, F7, F9 and F10 (help, find, caret browsing,
reader view, the menu), Tab (focus leaving the canvas) and a lone Alt. Only while the key's target is the canvas, or the
page with nothing else focused: in the page's own text fields, buttons and links the browser keeps every key. Shift+Tab
(the way out of an embedding iframe by keyboard), F6, Shift+F10, F5, F11, F12 and anything with Ctrl or Meta held
(paste) stay the browser's, and `runKaldra({ captureKeys: false })` leaves it every key. The app is sent every key either
way.

## Shader pipeline

Shaders are written in **Slang** and compiled offline to SPIR-V (Vulkan), signed DXIL (DirectX 12), and WGSL (WebGPU) by the `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Sdk` MSBuild targets at build time. Reflection JSON is emitted alongside each compiled shader; the backend reads it at `DefineTechnique` time to derive descriptor-binding layouts without you specifying them. The Slang-side contract — the platform macros and the binding rules — is [`shader-authoring.md`](shader-authoring.md).

Engine shaders (blit, tonemap, auto-exposure) are **embedded** in the backend assemblies. Your app's shaders compile to **loose files** (`.spv`/`.dxil`/`.json`) copied to `shaders/` in the output directory.

## Backend selection

Backends self-register via `[ModuleInitializer]` into `Backends.Available` (an `IReadOnlyList<IRenderBackend>`). Including a backend assembly in your project is enough to make it available; which one runs is a runtime decision — the host picks a registered backend by name (`Backends.Available.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Name == settings.PreferredBackend)`) and calls `backend.Create(surface, width, height, settings)`, handing over the window's native surface (Vulkan `IVkSurface` / DirectX 12 `HWND`).

When using `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Sdk` (NuGet or submodule), the `UseVulkan` / `UseDirectX12` / `UseWebGPU` MSBuild properties control which backend assemblies are referenced and therefore which `[ModuleInitializer]` calls fire; `UseVysara` / `UseImGui` do the same for the UI bridges.

## Threading: one thread records

**Everything that touches the recording path happens on one thread — the one that created the engine.** That means `Render`, `SetGraph`, and the whole `Write` family (`Write(Material, …)`, `Write(ConstantsHandle, …)`, `Write(StorageBufferHandle, …)`). This is not a lock you can take; nothing in that path is externally synchronized. A backend's command pool and queue are not synchronized objects in Vulkan or DirectX 12, and the engine's per-frame shadow buffers are plain dictionaries. A second thread does not contend — it corrupts, usually in a way that surfaces far from the call responsible.

Debug builds enforce it: `EngineBase.AssertRenderThread` compares the calling thread against the one that ran the constructor and throws naming both. It is `[Conditional("DEBUG")]` because it is a contract violation to fix in development, not a cost to carry in a shipped frame loop.

The deliberate exception is **asset creation**. `CreateTextureAsync`, `CreateMeshAsync` and their siblings may be called from any thread — a background image decode, a demo preloading concurrently — because they queue the GPU work rather than doing it. `ServicePendingUploads` drains that queue on the render thread. That single seam exists precisely because the rest of the surface has this affinity: without it, every background loader would need to marshal its own results.

Creation and release also have a *when*: between frames. Every create and release verb throws when the render thread calls it from inside a pass callback — an upload made while a frame records is submitted only ahead of the next frame, so the frame being recorded would sample memory its contents have not reached, and a release could free what that frame already draws with. A background thread queuing an upload through a `*Async` creator while a frame records is exactly what that seam is for, and is let through.

This is worth knowing before refactoring a backend toward parallel command recording. The contract is not an accident of the current implementation — the ordering it buys is load-bearing. `Write` provably runs before `Render` and outside command recording, which is what lets a growable storage buffer reallocate in place (see `EngineBase.GrowStorageBuffer`): there is no command buffer open to invalidate.

## What a new backend has to write

Most of a backend is not API code. The per-frame sequence, the derived plan's interpretation, and the draw-list state machine are the same everywhere, so they live once — in `EngineBase` and in `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Hosting` — and a backend inherits them.

`EngineBase.RecordFrame` owns the frame's shape: flush the app-writable buffer shadows, then per pass its debug-label scope, its derived transitions, its timestamps and its own recording, then close the trailing labels, copy the readback targets, and finish the frame. The order is the point. Each step has to happen in that sequence on every backend — a pass's barriers before its opening timestamp, because those barriers are the cost of the transition rather than of the pass; the readback copies before the frame's tail, because the tail may transition the very targets being copied — and a transliterated sequence is a sequence that can drift. It had: two backends recorded readback then capture and the third recorded capture then readback.

So a new backend implements hooks, not a loop:

| Hook | What it does |
|---|---|
| `WriteConstantsShadow` / `WriteStorageShadow` | Upload one app-writable buffer's bytes for this frame |
| `EmitTransitions` | Translate the derived `ResourceTransition`s (an API that tracks state itself overrides this as an explicit no-op) |
| `RecordComputePass` / `RecordRasterPass` | Open a scope over the pass's derived attachments and run its callback |
| `RecordReadback` | Copy each `g.Readback` target into this slot's buffer |
| `FinishFrame` | The capture, if requested, and the derived final transitions |
| `BeginLabel` / `EndLabel` | Open and close a named scope for a capture tool (or empty, deliberately) |
| `BeginFrameTimestamps` / `WritePassBeginTimestamp` / `WritePassEndTimestamp` / `EndFrameTimestamps` | Per-pass GPU timing (virtual — a backend with no timer implements none) |

`RecordRasterPass` stays whole to the backend rather than being templated further. Its attachment descriptors, formats and views are almost entirely API structs, and forcing them into one signature is exactly what would push graphics types into `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph`. What it inherits instead is the loop around it, the label bookkeeping, the transition emission, the timing index arithmetic, and `GraphPass.ResourceIdsWith` for the buffers a pass reads.

Draw lists are handled the same way. `DrawListWalker` decodes a submission's `DrawCommand` stream into steps — `Draw`, `BeginLayer`, `EndLayer` — and owns the group-opacity nesting, the nesting cap and its symmetric suppression, the scissor, the fully-clipped skip, and the per-command texture memoisation. `DrawListGeometry` answers the geometry: a layer's bounds, its target-pixel area, the composite quad, and the marker tag values the producer encodes. A backend's `DrawList` is then a `while (walker.MoveNext())` over three cases, each one just the API calls that step needs. A layer's identity is its **depth** — every backend's layer pool is indexed by depth already, so none of them keeps a stack of its own.

Resources split the same way. `EngineBase` owns the public create and release verbs and their neutral rules — refused while a pass records, and a texture a `Material` holds cannot be released — and a backend implements the GPU half:

| Hook | What it does |
|---|---|
| `UploadMesh` / `UploadSkinnedMesh` / `UploadTexture` | Upload and mint a handle. Ids start at 1 and are never reused, so `default` and stale handles fail loudly |
| `RetireMesh` / `RetireTexture` | Kill the handle at once; free the memory once no frame in flight — and no pending upload — can read it, on whatever schedule the API needs (a frame number, a fence value, or nothing: WebGPU's `destroy()` waits for submitted work itself) |

A backend that caches binding objects keyed by the handles of what they name — Vulkan's descriptor sets, WebGPU's bind groups — keys them with `BindingKey` in a `BindingCache`, whose invariant is that nothing an entry names is destroyed while the entry is cached. A whole generation dies at a drained moment (graph swap, resize, shader reload) and the cache is cleared; a single object dies at a retire, which evicts the entries naming it before its handle can be reused. That matters most where handles are recycled at once, as WebGPU's table indices are.

What is deliberately *not* shared is `*RenderContext.Verbs.cs`. Those files are ~90% descriptor-set, root-signature and bind-group construction; the only neutral part is a small geometry-source switch, which is not worth an abstraction. Policy differences between backends' record paths belong in `RecordValidator`, which exists for exactly that and is already one implementation.

The neutral floors a backend can rely on rather than re-check are in `GraphLimits` — uniform and storage reads per pass, colour attachments per pass — and derivation rejects a graph that exceeds them before any frame is recorded. `EngineCapabilities` reports the headroom a particular device has above those floors.

---

# Kaldra API Vocabulary

A reference for every key type in Kaldra's public API — *how to use it*. You author against `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core` (the Describe layer); the engine derives ordering, barriers, layout transitions, and aliasing for you. Verbs read as intent — you state what a pass reads and writes, never the order.

## Graph description (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Graph`)

A graph is built once with `RenderGraph.Define(g => { … })` and set on the engine with `engine.SetGraph`. The closure receives a `GraphBuilder` (`g`); you declare domains, resources, and passes on it.

| Type / member | Role |
|---|---|
| `RenderGraph.Define(g => …)` | The one entry point: runs the authoring closure and returns an immutable, hashable `RenderGraph`. Hand it to `engine.SetGraph`. |
| `g.Pass("name")` | Begin a raster pass → `PassBuilder`. Chain access verbs, then `.Draw(ctx => …)`. |
| `g.Compute("name")` | Begin a compute pass → `PassBuilder`. Chain access verbs, then `.Dispatch(ctx => …)`. |
| `g.Present(colorHandle)` | The terminal: declare which colour resource is shown this frame (returns void). |
| `g.Readback(handle)` | Declare a GPU→CPU readback of a resource; returns the same handle. Read it later with `engine.Read`. |
| `using (g.Scope("name"))` | Prefix every domain/resource/pass declared in the block with `name.`, so a reusable fragment can be instantiated more than once. Nests. Techniques and the backbuffer are not scoped. |
| `g.Buffer<T>("name", count)` | A GPU storage buffer of `count × sizeof(T)` (not resolution-bound) → `BufferHandle`. |
| `g.Buffer("name", count, layout)` | The same, sized by a `VertexLayout`'s stride — the spelling for a buffer a compute fills and a draw consumes as its per-instance stream. Naming the layout the technique names lets the draw path reject a stride mismatch. |
| `g.Buffer("name", byteSize)` | The same as an opaque block of `byteSize` bytes. Declares no element contract, so neither draw-path guard applies — prefer one of the two above. |
| `g.Constants<T>("name")` | An app-written uniform/constant block of `sizeof(T)` bytes → `ConstantsHandle`. Fill with `engine.Write`. |
| `g.Storage<T>("name", count, growable=false)` | An app-written structured array (SSBO), `count × sizeof(T)` → `StorageBufferHandle`. `growable: true` lets a larger `Write` grow it. A `Constants` or `Storage` buffer is uploaded only into the frame slots behind its last `Write`, so one written once costs nothing per frame however large it is; the last `Write` persists either way. |
| `g.Persistent("name", format, size=1)` | A screen-sized cross-frame colour image whose memory is never aliased → `ColorHandle`. Only `size == 1` is supported. A window resize reallocates it at the new extent, so its contents are lost (there is no resample) — use `domain.Persistent` on a fixed-size domain for history that must outlive a resize. |

### Pass access declarations (`PassBuilder`, all chainable)

You declare intent; the engine derives ordering, barriers, and layout transitions.

| Verb | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `.Writes(params ColorHandle[])` | Produce colour target(s) (the engine may clear). Multiple handles = MRT. |
| `.Blends(ColorHandle)` | Read-modify-write: load existing contents + blend onto them (the pass is last reader and next writer). |
| `.Samples(params ITextureHandle[])` | Bind colour/depth image(s) as shader-read (sampled) inputs. |
| `.WritesDepth(DepthHandle)` / `.ReadsDepth(DepthHandle)` | Depth write / depth test without write. |
| `.ReadWrites(params IStorageHandle[])` | Read-modify-write storage images or buffers (compute UAV). |
| `.ReadsVertex(BufferHandle)` | Bind a buffer as a vertex / instance stream (a compute pass filled it). |
| `.ReadsIndirect(BufferHandle)` | Bind a buffer as draw arguments — the counts the command processor reads instead of the CPU supplying them. |
| `.Reads(IUniformHandle)` | Read a `g.Constants` block as the technique's uniform input, in a raster pass or a compute pass alike: a technique's constant buffers take the pass's blocks in the order read, and a compute technique declaring more than its pass reads throws at dispatch. |
| `.Reads(IStorageBufferHandle)` | Read a `g.Storage` SSBO read-only (an overload of `.Reads`). Bound to every draw in the pass, mesh or fullscreen, **by position**: a technique's first storage buffer takes the first the pass reads, its second the second, and so on, as many as it declares (vertex or fragment stage) — never by name. So a technique that reads only some of a pass's storage buffers must declare them in the order the pass reads them, from its first: one that declares only the pass's second gets its first. Where the element sizes show it (a slot's reflected element against the buffer's `sizeof(T)`, packed or padded to its std430 alignment), that throws at the draw, naming both; one declaring more than the pass reads throws too. A material draw whose technique reads storage throws, on every backend. In a compute pass the technique's read-only storage buffers (`StructuredBuffer<T>`) take them by the same rule, and its read-write ones the dispatch's own storage; one declaring more read-only buffers than its pass reads, or more read-write ones than the dispatch supplies, throws at dispatch. A read-only slot binds only the pass's `.Reads` storage, so a GPU-produced `g.Buffer` a dispatch supplies must be declared `RWStructuredBuffer` in the shader even when it is only read. |
| `.Queue(Queue)` | Assign the pass to a queue (see `Queue` below). |
| `.Draw(Action<IRenderContext>)` / `.Dispatch(Action<IRenderContext>)` | The per-frame record callback (raster / compute). Pull from `ctx`; never capture per-frame data. |

### Special handles & domains

`Domain`s decide where each resource lives. Declare a colour/depth target *on* a domain — there is no standalone `g.Color`.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `g.Backbuffer` | The swapchain colour target (`ColorHandle`) — *is* the present surface. Hand it to `.Writes`/`.Blends` and `g.Present`. |
| `g.Screen` | The native-resolution `Domain` (alias for `g.Backbuffer.Domain`); declare full-res sibling targets here. |
| `g.Domain("name", width, height, samples=1)` | A fixed-size `Domain` (a constant-size pixel-art world); `samples` is the MSAA count (power of two, within `Capabilities.SampleCounts`: WebGPU has 1 and 4). Every target in a multisampled domain is multisampled, and so is every pipeline drawing into it. A pass that `.Samples` a multisampled colour target reads its *resolve*: the engine resolves it into a single-sample image of its own wherever the graph takes it from being drawn to being sampled, so nothing in the graph names the resolve. Anything else is refused when the graph is derived, the same on every backend: sampling a multisampled depth target, `.ReadWrites` on a multisampled target (a storage image is single-sample), `g.Readback` or `g.Present` of one, and a `Persistent` target in a multisampled domain. Group-opacity UI layers drawn in a multisampled pass render single-sample and composite back at the pass's count. |
| `g.Domain("name", scale, samples=1)` | A backbuffer-relative `Domain` — `scale × native`, re-resolved on resize (e.g. `0.5f` for half-res). |
| `domain.Color("name", format, clearValue?=null, noClear?=false)` | A colour target in this domain → `ColorHandle`. `noClear: true` skips the clear (only when the first pass covers every pixel). |
| `domain.Color("name", format, scale, …)` | A colour target at a fraction of the domain's resolution (mip chains, bloom pyramid). |
| `domain.Depth("name", format, clearDepth = 1f, noClear = false)` | A depth target in this domain → `DepthHandle`. `clearDepth: 0f` is the reversed-Z far plane; `noClear` skips the clear (only correct when the first depth-writing pass covers every pixel). |
| `domain.Persistent("name", format)` | A cross-frame target sized to this domain (use a tiny domain for a scalar history). On a fixed-size domain its contents survive a window resize; on a backbuffer-relative one it is reallocated like any other screen-sized target. |
| `g.BackbufferClear` / `g.BackbufferNoClear` | Set the backbuffer's first-write clear colour / skip the clear — before the first `g.Backbuffer` access. |

So a target is declared `g.Screen.Color("hdr", Format.Rgba16F)` or `g.Screen.Depth("depth", Format.Depth32F)`.

### `Format` (render-graph attachment formats, `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Graph`)

The complete set of attachment/target formats:

| Format | Typical use |
|---|---|
| `Rgba8Srgb` | sRGB colour the eye reads directly (the default backbuffer encoding). |
| `Rgba8Unorm` | 8-bit RGBA linear data (packed material params). |
| `Bgra8Srgb` | The channel-swapped sibling of `Rgba8Srgb` — the backbuffer takes it where the platform's preferred swapchain or canvas format is BGRA (most WebGPU canvases). |
| `Rgb10A2` | 10/10/10/2 packed — cheap higher-precision normals. |
| `Rgba16F` | HDR colour with range for bloom. |
| `R16F` | Single-channel float — SSAO, the exposure scalar, small object-id picking. |
| `R32F` | Single-channel full-precision float — the only single-channel float WebGPU allows as a read-write storage texture (the auto-exposure scalar). |
| `R32Uint` | Single-channel 32-bit uint — exact integer object ids of any range. |
| `Rg16F` | Two-channel float — velocity, JFA seed coordinates. |
| `Depth32F` | 32-bit float depth. |

`format.BytesPerTexel` and `format.IsFilterableFloat` (`FormatExtensions`) answer the two questions every backend needs the same answer to: a readback's texel size, and whether a shader can read the format through a filtering float sampler on every backend (false for `Depth32F`, `R32Uint` and `R32F`).

### `Queue` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Graph`)

`Queue.Graphics` (the default for every pass) and `Queue.AsyncCompute`. `AsyncCompute` is reserved for a future multi-queue scheduler — assigning it currently fails loudly at derive time rather than silently running on the graphics queue.

## Authoring a graph

```csharp
var graph = RenderGraph.Define(g =>
{
    var screen   = g.Backbuffer;                              // the swapchain target
    var depth    = g.Screen.Depth("depth", Format.Depth32F);
    var viewProj = g.Constants<Matrix4x4>("camera.viewproj"); // a per-frame uniform channel

    g.Pass("opaque")
        .Reads(viewProj)             // declared inputs/outputs — ordering & barriers are derived
        .Writes(screen)
        .WritesDepth(depth)
        .Draw(ctx =>
        {
            foreach (var obj in visibleObjects)        // your own culled draw list, however you build it
            {
                var call = DrawCall.Create(obj.Mesh, "lit");
                call.Material = obj.Material;
                var model = obj.ModelMatrix;
                call.SetUniforms(ref model);           // a per-draw block, matching the shader's cbuffer
                ctx.Draw(call);
            }
        });

    g.Present(screen);
});
engine.SetGraph(graph);
```

Ping-pong (bloom, JFA) is just two handles and a `(read, write)` tuple swapped in a normal loop — the graph follows the handles. View, light, and time data flow in through `g.Constants`/`g.Storage` channels a pass `.Reads`; the engine names no game concept.

## Engine hosting (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Hosting`)

| Type | Role |
|---|---|
| `Backends` | Static backend registry. `Backends.Available` is an `IReadOnlyList<IRenderBackend>` (registration order); each referenced backend assembly self-registers as it loads. |
| `IRenderBackend` | A discoverable backend: `string Name` and `IEngine Create(object surface, int width, int height, EngineSettings settings)`. The surface is opaque (Vulkan `IVkSurface` / DX12 `HWND`). |
| `IEngine` | The live engine — owns the device and pipeline cache, survives graph swaps. See its members below. |
| `IRenderContext` | The per-frame execution context passed to `.Draw` / `.Dispatch`. Closures *pull* from it rather than capturing. |
| `EngineSettings` | Backend-neutral engine config (subclass per backend). |
| `FrameInputs` | The per-frame host data handed to `IEngine.Render`. |
| `TechniqueDescriptor` | A backend-neutral technique definition (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials`), registered with `IEngine.DefineTechnique`. |

### Selecting a backend and creating the engine

```csharp
var backend = Backends.Available.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Name == settings.PreferredBackend)
              ?? Backends.Available.First();
using var engine = backend.Create(window.Surface, width, height, settings);
```

`Backends.Available` is a list, not a dictionary — select by `Name`, never an indexer. Constructing a backend's `EngineSettings` subclass (`VulkanEngineSettings` / `DirectX12EngineSettings`) is what loads and registers that backend.

### Input on the desktop (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Hosting.Desktop`)

The host turns the window's devices into `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Input`'s neutral `InputEvent` stream: keyboards and mice through
GLFW (`DesktopInputPump`), gamepads through SDL 3 (`SdlGamepadPump`), or through GLFW where SDL is missing or won't start.

| Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `HostOptions.Pads` (`--pads sdl\|glfw`) | Where gamepads are read from: `GamepadSource.Sdl` (default) or `GamepadSource.Glfw`. |
| `SdlGamepadPump` | SDL's gamepad subsystem alone (no SDL window), pumped once a frame on the host's thread: SDL's own drivers where it has them (DualSense and DualShock over HID, with rumble; Switch pads; the Steam Controller without Steam), XInput and Windows.Gaming.Input pads otherwise. Pads keep the lowest free of the four slots while connected. The host's focus gates its events: unfocused, held buttons are released; focused again, each pad is read afresh. |
| `DesktopInputPump(…, gamepads: false)` | Keyboards and mice alone, when SDL has the pads, so no pad is seen twice. |
| `GamepadState.Type`, `.Family`, `.Vendor`, `.Product` | What a pad is, for prompts that name its buttons: a `GamepadType` (SDL's list: Xbox 360 and One, PS3–PS5, Switch Pro, Joy-Cons, GameCube, Steam, or `Unknown`), its `GamepadFamily` (whose labels its face buttons carry: Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, Steam), and its USB ids where the host has them. Carried by `InputEvent.GamepadConnected(pad, type, vendor, product)`: SDL gives the real type (behind Steam's virtual pad too), GLFW only its mapping's name, a browser its `Gamepad.id`; `GamepadIdentity` reads ids, names and ids' strings. |
| `InputSnapshot.LastDevice`, `.LastPad` | The device the player last used (keyboard, mouse, a pad, touch), for prompts that follow what is in hand: moved by a key or button going down, the wheel, a mouse moved more than 8 px, a stick past 0.4 or a trigger past 0.3, never by drift. |
| `Pad.Last` | The pad index meaning the pad last used (the first connected before any is). Every `Pad` helper and every implicit pad binding reads it, and so do `InputSnapshot.Down/Pressed/Released(GamepadButton)`, so whichever pad is picked up drives; `Pad.OnPad` pins a binding to one pad. |
| `InputBinding.Controls()`, `InputControl` | A binding broken into the physical controls it reads, in order (a composite's keys; a stick; the trigger pair), for drawing a glyph per control. `InputControl.Name(GamepadType)` names one as the pad in hand prints it ("Cross", "R2", "Create" on a DualSense; "A", "RT", "View" on an Xbox pad; "Left grip" on a Steam Controller); `ToBinding()` makes a binding of one. |
| `InputSnapshot.Touches`, `TouchPoint` | The touch contacts this frame, each by a stable `Id`: its `Position` now and at the frame's start (`Previous`, `Delta`), where it came down (`Start`), and its `Phase`: `Began` for the frame it came down in, then `Moved` or `Stationary`, then `Ended` or `Canceled` for one frame (`Gone`). A tap that comes and goes within one frame is reported once, ended, with `BeganThisFrame`. A touch is never a mouse: hosts send each finger as `InputEventKind.Touch`. |
| `Win32TouchPump` (desktop host) | A touch screen on Windows, which GLFW doesn't read: the window's procedure subclassed for `WM_POINTER` messages, each finger a contact in client pixels, and a touch handled there never promoted to a mouse; the touch feedback Windows draws is turned off for the window. A pen and the mouse go on to GLFW. The browser host reads the canvas's pointer events instead, with `touch-action: none` over it. |
| `InputActions.Press(action)` | Presses a button action from outside its bindings (an on-screen button, a tap on a prompt): the next `Resolve` finds it held, so it is pressed that frame and released the next, whatever its bindings are. |
| `InputActions.Names`, `KindOf`, `Bindings`, `Defaults`, `ResetToDefaults`, `ActionsUsing(control)` | For a rebinding screen: each action and what it reads now and as defined; putting one or all back; which actions already read a control. |
| `BindingCapture` | "Press a key": started from the snapshot as it is (whatever is held then is ignored until let go), polled each frame until a fresh key, mouse button, pad button, trigger past half way or stick direction past 0.6 from the families asked for (`Captured`, `Pad`), or the cancel key or button. |
| `GamepadButton.Misc1`, `RightPaddle1`, `LeftPaddle1`, `RightPaddle2`, `LeftPaddle2`, `Touchpad` | The buttons past the standard fifteen: a DualSense's mic button and touchpad click, a Steam Controller's grips (paddle 1 each side), an Elite's or DualSense Edge's paddles. GLFW and the browser report none of them. |

SDL 3 comes from the `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.SDL3` package ([Kaldra.SDL3](https://github.com/AtomicBlom/Kaldra.SDL3)):
SDL's own release builds of `SDL3.dll` for win-x64 and win-arm64, with its licence, versioned as SDL is (3.4.20 is SDL
3.4.20). It carries no bindings. Where it has no build (anywhere but Windows), the host reads pads through GLFW. Our
own binding (`Sdl3`) is `[LibraryImport]` over blittable signatures only.

### `EngineSettings`

| Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `EnableValidation` | Enable the backend's validation/debug layer (on by default; degrades gracefully if absent). |
| `VSync` | Paced, tear-free present; when false the backend uses its lowest-latency present mode. |
| `MaxFramesPerSecond` | Frame-rate cap (0 = unlimited; only meaningful with `VSync` off). |
| `HdrOutput` | Request an HDR-capable swapchain + HDR output transform, falling back to SDR. |
| `PreferredBackend` | The backend `Name` to select (null = the first available). |
| `WatchShaderDirectory` | Hot-reload loose shaders rebuilt on disk (dev-only; off by default). |

`VulkanEngineSettings` adds `ShaderDirectory` and `PreferDiscreteGpu`. `DirectX12EngineSettings` adds `ShaderDirectory`, `PreferDiscreteGpu`, and `GpuBasedValidation` (on in Debug, off in Release).

### `IEngine` members

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `BackendName` / `DeviceName` | The backend name (e.g. `"Vulkan"`) and a human-readable GPU name. |
| `DefineTechnique(name, TechniqueDescriptor)` | Register a technique under a logical name passes reference. Idempotent per name. |
| `CreateMesh(ReadOnlySpan<Vertex>, ReadOnlySpan<uint> indices)` | Upload geometry in the canonical `MeshStandard` layout → `Mesh`. Between frames only: throws inside a pass. |
| `CreateMesh<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T>, VertexLayout, ReadOnlySpan<uint>)` | Upload geometry with an explicit layout (`sizeof(T) == layout.Stride`). |
| `CreateSkinnedMesh(ReadOnlySpan<SkinnedVertex>, ReadOnlySpan<uint>)` | Upload a skinned bind-pose mesh (readable by the compute pre-skin) → `Mesh`. |
| `ReleaseMesh(Mesh)` | Kill a mesh's handle at once; its buffers are freed once no frame in flight can read them. Between frames only. |
| `CreateInstances<T>(span, layout)` | Upload per-instance data once, to GPU-resident memory, for draws to take ranges of (`DrawCall.Static`): instances that don't change from frame to frame, which a CPU span would upload every frame. `sizeof(T)` must be the layout's stride. |
| `ReleaseInstances(InstanceBuffer)` | Free one, under `ReleaseMesh`'s rules. |
| `CreateTexture(TextureData)` | Upload an image + mip chain → `Texture`. Between frames only: an upload made inside a pass would miss the frame that samples it, so it throws there. |
| `CreateTextureAsync(TextureData)` | Queue an upload from any thread; completes when `ServicePendingUploads` (called by `Render`) drains it. |
| `ReleaseTexture(Texture)` | Kill a texture's handle at once; its image is destroyed once no frame in flight can read it. Throws for a texture a `Material` holds, and inside a pass. |
| `UpdateTexture(Texture, ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` | Write a whole new image into a texture in place, ahead of the next frame; frames in flight keep what they had. The handle, materials and bindings stay, and nothing allocates after a texture's first update. One mip level and one layer only, texels exactly its size; between frames only. |
| `CreateMaterial(params ReadOnlySpan<Texture>)` | Bundle textures (in the shader's binding order) → `Material`. A material holds its textures for the engine's lifetime. |
| `AllocateDrawListStream()` | Mint an engine-unique stream id for a stable `DrawListIdentity`, so draw-list producers never share kept geometry. |
| `SetGraph(RenderGraph)` | Make a graph active — derive its schedule/barriers/aliasing, reusing device + pipeline cache. Safe to call again to swap graphs. |
| `Write<T>(ConstantsHandle, in T)` | Write a value into a `g.Constants` buffer (reaches the reading pass on the next frame). |
| `Write<T>(StorageBufferHandle, ReadOnlySpan<T>)` | Write an array into a `g.Storage` buffer (the span counterpart). |
| `Render(FrameInputs)` | Render one frame of the active graph. |
| `Resize(int width, int height)` | Notify the engine the output surface resized (drives swapchain + relative-domain recreation). |
| `Read(ResourceHandle)` | Read back a `g.Readback` target's CPU copy as tightly-packed bytes (a frame or two old; empty before populated). |
| `RequestCapture(string path)` | Capture the next presented frame to a PNG (debug/validation). |
| `GpuTimingEnabled` | Toggle per-pass GPU timestamp collection (off by default; no graph rebuild). |
| `LastFrameTimings` / `LastFrameGpuMilliseconds` | Per-pass timings and total GPU time of the most recently completed frame. |
| `ResourceInspectionEnabled` / `InspectableResources` | Enable the resource viewer (set before `SetGraph`) and list the inspectable images. |
| `WaitIdle()` | Block until the GPU is idle (call before disposing host-owned resources). |

### `IRenderContext` members

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `Time` / `DeltaTime` | Elapsed seconds since startup / since the previous frame. |
| `HdrOutput` | `true` when the engine negotiated an HDR display output. |
| `Frame` | The frame being recorded: 0 for the engine's first `Render`, one more for each after, the same in every pass of a frame. |
| `FullScreen(technique, params ReadOnlySpan<ResourceHandle> inputs)` | Draw a fullscreen triangle, binding `inputs` as the technique's sampled inputs 0..N-1. |
| `FullScreen(technique, ReadOnlySpan<float> push, params ReadOnlySpan<ResourceHandle> inputs)` | As above, plus a small inline fragment-stage scalar block. |
| `Dispatch(technique, (uint X, uint Y, uint Z) groups, ReadOnlySpan<float> push, ReadOnlySpan<ResourceHandle> sampled, ReadOnlySpan<ResourceHandle> storage)` | Dispatch a compute technique over a workgroup grid. |
| `Draw(in DrawCall call)` | Submit one raster draw (the unified draw verb — see `DrawCall`). |
| `DispatchSkin(technique, Mesh skinnedMesh, ReadOnlySpan<Matrix4x4> palette, BufferHandle output, int vertexCount)` | Compute pre-skin a bind pose by a bone palette into `output` (a `.ReadWrites` buffer). |
| `DrawList<TVertex>(technique, DrawListIdentity identity, ReadOnlySpan<TextureRef> textures, ReadOnlySpan<TVertex> vertices, ReadOnlySpan<ushort> indices, ReadOnlySpan<DrawCommand> commands, ReadOnlySpan<float> push)` | Submit a batched indexed draw list (the overlay/UI path). Each command samples `textures[TextureIndex]` — an engine `Texture` or a graph texture (see `TextureRef`). `identity` is `DrawListIdentity.Transient` for a list rebuilt every frame, or a minted stream + revision for one whose geometry the backend may keep. |
| `ResolveInspectable(int resourceId)` | Resolve an inspectable resource id to a `Texture?` bindable in a draw list this frame — the resource viewer's hook, which needs no `.Samples` because inspection keeps every inspectable resource sampleable. |

### `FrameInputs`

A fresh value per frame (a `readonly record struct`, no allocation). The single channel for everything frame-varying — there is no engine `Camera`/`Sun`/`Scene`:

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `DeltaSeconds` (`double`) | Seconds since the previous frame; surfaced as `ctx.DeltaTime`. |
| `Time` (`double`) | Elapsed seconds since startup; surfaced as `ctx.Time`. |

View-projections, light, and time-of-day data are *not* here — publish them through `g.Constants`/`g.Storage` with `engine.Write(handle, value)` and read them in a pass with `.Reads`.

### `TechniqueDescriptor` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials`)

A record naming a shader *logically* and stating its pipeline intent; descriptor-binding counts are reflected from the shader, so you never hand-count them.

```csharp
engine.DefineTechnique("lit", new TechniqueDescriptor("lit", HasVertexInput: true));

// instanced, back-face culled, drawn from the Transform per-instance layout
engine.DefineTechnique("foliage", new TechniqueDescriptor("foliage",
    HasVertexInput: true,
    Instance: VertexLayout.Transform,
    Cull: CullMode.Back));
```

| Parameter (default) | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Shader` | Logical shader name; the backend resolves bytecode + reflection. |
| `VertexEntry` (`"vertexMain"`) / `FragmentEntry` (`"fragmentMain"`) | Entry-point names. For a compute technique the single entry point sits in `FragmentEntry`. |
| `HasVertexInput` (`false`) | Reads a vertex stream (a mesh) vs fabricating a fullscreen triangle. |
| `Blend` (`BlendMode.None`) | Blend equation — pairs with a `.Blends` pass. |
| `LinearFilter` (`false`) | Sample inputs with linear vs nearest filtering. |
| `HasFragmentPush` (`false`) | The fragment/compute stage reads a small inline scalar block (up to sixteen floats). |
| `IsCompute` (`false`) | A compute technique — one entry point, dispatched not drawn. |
| `Address` (`SamplerAddress.Clamp`) | Sampler wrap mode for out-of-range coordinates. |
| `Layout` (`null`) | The per-vertex `VertexLayout` (defaults to `MeshStandard` when `HasVertexInput`). |
| `Instance` (`null`) | The per-instance `VertexLayout` (e.g. `Transform`) for instanced draws. |
| `HasListPush` (`false`) | A draw-list technique's all-stage push block (whose last slot each command's `Tag` rewrites). |
| `Cull` (`CullMode.None`) | Which faces the rasterizer discards — front faces are counter-clockwise. |
| `DepthTest` (`DepthCompare.LessOrEqual`) | The depth comparison a fragment must pass, when the pass has a depth target. |
| `Bias` (`null`) | A constant + slope-scaled depth offset (`DepthBias`) — the shadow-acne knob. |
| `AlphaToCoverage` (`false`) | In a multisampled pass, the fragment's alpha decides how many of its samples it covers, so a cut-out (a leaf, a fence's wire) is edged as smoothly as geometry rather than stepped by a discard. How alpha becomes a sample mask is the driver's choice and differs between APIs on one GPU, so such edges aren't at pixel parity across backends. No effect in a pass of one sample. |
| `SampleCompare` (`null`) | The compare function of the shader's comparison samplers: a `Sampler2DShadow` read with `SampleCmp` passes where `reference [compare] stored` (a reversed-depth shadow map takes `GreaterOrEqual`). Which inputs compare is found in the shader (its SPIR-V's depth-comparison samples; WebGPU's `sampler_comparison`); they get a filtered (2×2 PCF), edge-clamped comparison sampler and the rest keep `LinearFilter`'s. A shader that compares without it, or a technique naming it whose shader doesn't, throws at `DefineTechnique`, as does a comparison the SPIR-V can't trace to its texture (one through a local, a phi or a function parameter). The compared texture is a depth target the pass `.Samples`: a material's textures are colour formats, which no backend compares, so a material for a comparing technique throws at `CreateMaterial` or at the draw, and so does a draw-list technique naming `SampleCompare`. |

Shaders are authored in **Slang** and compiled offline to SPIR-V (Vulkan), signed DXIL (DirectX 12), and WGSL (WebGPU) with reflection JSON. The Slang-side half of the contract — the platform macros, the two independent numbering schemes, and where a push block actually lands — is [`shader-authoring.md`](shader-authoring.md).

### Pipeline-intent enums

| Enum (`namespace`) | Members |
|---|---|
| `BlendMode` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Graph`) | `None`, `AlphaOver`, `Additive`, `PremultipliedAlpha`, `Multiply`. |
| `CullMode` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Graph`) | `None`, `Back`, `Front` (front faces are counter-clockwise). |
| `DepthCompare` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Graph`) | `Never`, `Less`, `Equal`, `LessOrEqual`, `Greater`, `NotEqual`, `GreaterOrEqual`, `Always`. |
| `SamplerAddress` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials`) | `Clamp`, `Repeat`, `MirrorRepeat`, `ClampToBorder`, `MirrorClampToEdge`. |

### Reversed-Z

Reversed-Z puts the far plane at depth 0, which cancels the perspective divide's precision loss at distance against a float depth buffer's density near zero — the standard fix for depth fighting in a large world. It is **three declarations that must agree**; getting one wrong doesn't fail, it inverts or erases occlusion:

```csharp
var depth = g.Screen.Depth("depth", Format.Depth32F, clearDepth: 0f);          // 1. far plane at 0
camera.Perspective(fovY, aspect, 0.1f, 5000f, reversed: true);                 // 2. reversed projection
engine.DefineTechnique("mesh", new TechniqueDescriptor("mesh",
    HasVertexInput: true, DepthTest: DepthCompare.GreaterOrEqual));            // 3. reversed test
```

Viewport `MinDepth`/`MaxDepth` stay `0`/`1` — the reversal lives in the projection, not the viewport.

**Depth bias is only partly portable.** `DepthBias.SlopeScale` means the same thing on every backend. `DepthBias.Constant` does not: Vulkan multiplies it by an implementation-defined `r`, D3D12 applies `Constant × 2^(exponent−23)` for a float depth buffer. Prefer the slope-scaled term, or tune the constant per backend.

## Drawing, instancing, skinning (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Hosting`)

`ctx.Draw(in DrawCall)` is the unified raster draw verb. `DrawCall` is a `ref struct`; build the common case with `DrawCall.Create(mesh, technique)`, or use an object initializer for richer calls.

| Member | Role |
|---|---|
| `DrawCall.Create(mesh, technique)` | The terse single-mesh, no-material case. |
| `Technique` (required `string`) | The technique that selects the pipeline. |
| `Mesh` (`Mesh?`) | The mesh to draw; `null` for procedural draws (set `VertexCount`). |
| `SkinnedVertices` (`BufferHandle?`) | A pre-skinned vertex buffer override (the mesh still supplies its indices); must be a `.ReadsVertex` buffer. |
| `VertexCount` (`int`) | Vertices per instance for procedural draws (when `Mesh` is null). |
| `Instances` (`InstanceSource`) | Per-instance data — empty (default) = single draw. |
| `Indices` (`IndexRange`) | Which sub-range of the mesh to draw; empty (default) = the whole mesh. |
| `Material` (`Material?`) | Material whose textures fill the technique's sampler slots; `null` for untextured techniques. |
| `Uniforms` / `.SetUniforms<T>(ref T)` / `.SetUniforms<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T>)` | The per-draw uniform block (raw bytes matching the shader's cbuffer); set it from a typed value or span. |
| `Sampled` (`ReadOnlySpan<ResourceHandle>`) | Graph resources bound as sampled inputs (each declared via `.Samples`). |
| `DrawCall.From<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T>)` | Build an `InstanceSource` from a CPU instance span (uploaded per frame). |
| `DrawCall.Gpu(BufferHandle, count)` | Build an `InstanceSource` from a GPU-resident buffer a compute pass filled. |
| `DrawCall.Static(InstanceBuffer, first, count)` | Build an `InstanceSource` from a range of instances uploaded once (`IEngine.CreateInstances`); nothing is uploaded per frame. The range is checked against the buffer, and the technique's instance stride against its stride. |
| `DrawCall.Indirect(BufferHandle, byteOffset)` | Build an `InstanceSource` whose counts come from a buffer (declared `.ReadsIndirect`); `Indices` is ignored — the range comes from the buffer. |
| `DrawCall.Range(firstIndex, indexCount, baseVertex)` | Build an `IndexRange`, so one mesh can hold several primitives. |

`InstanceSource` (a nested `ref struct`) exposes `IsEmpty` and `Count`; construct it only via `DrawCall.From` / `DrawCall.Gpu` / `DrawCall.Static` / `DrawCall.Indirect`. An indirect draw has no CPU-known `Count` — it reports zero, because only the GPU knows. Skinning is `ctx.DispatchSkin(...)` (a compute pre-skin into a `.ReadsVertex` buffer) followed by an ordinary `ctx.Draw` of that buffer.

## Geometry & materials

| Type (`namespace`) | Role |
|---|---|
| `Mesh` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | An opaque handle to uploaded geometry from `IEngine.CreateMesh` / `CreateSkinnedMesh`. Survives graph swaps; dies at `IEngine.ReleaseMesh`. |
| `InstanceBuffer` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | A handle to instances uploaded once by `IEngine.CreateInstances`: its count and stride, stored as a mesh is. Dies at `IEngine.ReleaseInstances`. |
| `Vertex` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | The canonical interleaved vertex — `record struct (Vector3 Position, Vector3 Normal, Vector2 Uv, Vector4 Tangent)`, 48 bytes. |
| `SkinnedVertex` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Animation`) | The skinned bind-pose vertex — `Vertex` fields plus four bone indices (`Joint0..3`) + `Vector4 Weights`, 80 bytes. |
| `OverlayVertex` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | The 2D overlay vertex (position, uv, premultiplied RGBA16F colour, custom) used by draw lists. |
| `viewProjection.TryProjectToScreen(world, viewportSize, clipSpaceCorrection, out screen, out depth)` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | Extension member on `Matrix4x4`: a world point → viewport pixels (top-left origin, +Y down) and NDC depth, through the view-projection an app hands its shaders. `clipSpaceCorrection` is `IEngine.ClipSpaceCorrection`, which says which way the backend's NDC Y runs, so the pixel is the same on every backend. False when the point is on or behind the eye's plane. |
| `viewProjection.TryUnprojectFromScreen(screen, depth, viewportSize, clipSpaceCorrection, out world)` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | The inverse: the world point under a viewport pixel at an NDC depth (0 and 1 give the near and far ends of its ray). |
| `viewProjection.GetFrustumCorners()` / `ToFrustum()` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | Extension members on `Matrix4x4`: the eight world-space frustum corners, and the six planes as a `Frustum`. |
| `VertexLayout` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Geometry`) | A backend-neutral per-stream attribute layout. Built-ins: `MeshStandard`, `MeshSkinned`, `Overlay`, `Transform` (the standard per-instance 4×4 matrix stream). |
| `Material` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials`) | An opaque `record struct (int Id)` — an ordered `Texture` bundle from `IEngine.CreateMaterial` that fills a technique's reflected sampler slots. |
| `Texture` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials`) | An opaque handle to an uploaded texture from `IEngine.CreateTexture`. Survives graph swaps; dies at `IEngine.ReleaseTexture`. Ids start at 1, so `default(Texture)` names nothing and is refused. |
| `TextureData` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials`) | A neutral image description (pixel data + mip chain). Built via `FromRgba8`, `FromRgba16F`, `FromCubeFaces`; carries `Format` (`TextureFormat`), `Width`, `Height`, `Levels`, `IsCube`. |
| `TextureFormat` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials`) | Source-image encoding (distinct from `Format`): `Rgba8Srgb`, `Rgba8Unorm`, `Rgba16F`. |

## Assets (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Assets`)

Neutral loaders beside `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core` (no graphics-API reference). They emit `TextureData` / `Vertex` arrays / a `Skeleton` / `AnimationClip`s; the app turns those into engine meshes, textures, and materials.

| Member | Role |
|---|---|
| `ImageLoader.Load(path, TextureFormat format, generateMips=true)` | Decode a PNG/JPG/… file to `TextureData` with a CPU mip chain. |
| `ImageLoader.Decode(Stream, TextureFormat, generateMips=true)` | Decode an encoded image from a stream (e.g. a glTF-embedded image). |
| `ImageLoader.LoadHdr(path)` / `ImageLoader.DecodeHdr(Stream)` | Decode a Radiance HDR / float image to `Rgba16F` `TextureData`. |
| `GltfLoader.Load(path)` | Load a glTF/GLB model → `LoadedModel`. |
| `LoadedModel` | `Primitives` (`IReadOnlyList<ModelPrimitive>`), `Skeleton?`, `Clips` (`IReadOnlyList<AnimationClip>`). |
| `ModelPrimitive` | `Vertices` (`Vertex[]`), `Indices` (`uint[]`), `Material` (`ModelMaterial?`), `SkinnedVertices` (`SkinnedVertex[]?`), `IsSkinned`. |

## Overlay draw lists (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Hosting`)

The cross-backend verb behind overlay/UI-style rendering (game UI via Vysara, ImGui, debug lines): a pass stages a per-frame, variable-size indexed vertex stream and submits it with `ctx.DrawList<TVertex>(...)`. There is no `FrameInputs`/`ctx` channel for this — a pass gets its geometry from whatever stable producer it holds as pass state (a painter), reading its live contents each frame.

| Type | Role |
|---|---|
| `DrawCommand` | One run within a list — `record struct (Rect ClipRect, int TextureIndex, int IndexOffset, int IndexCount, int VertexOffset, uint Tag)`. `Tag` is the per-command value a list-push technique reads. |
| `DrawListIdentity` | `record struct (int Stream, uint Revision)` — which kept geometry stream a list is and which revision of it. `Transient` (revision 0) keeps nothing; a stable stream comes from `IEngine.AllocateDrawListStream()` and is refused otherwise, because two producers sharing one would draw each other's geometry. |
| `TextureRef` | What one slot of a list samples: an engine `Texture` (implicit from `Texture`) or a graph texture an earlier pass rendered this frame (implicit from `ColorHandle`/`DepthHandle`, or `new TextureRef(ITextureHandle)`). A value type, so a producer keeps an array of them and rewrites it in place. A graph texture is an ordinary sampled input: the submitting pass declares it with `.Samples` or the list throws `PassBindingException`, and its format must sample as a filterable float (`Format.IsFilterableFloat`), so a depth, integer or `R32F` target is refused on every backend. The backend resolves it to the live image each submission, so a resize needs nothing from the caller. |

A list that shows a target the frame rendered — a minimap, a portal, a render-to-texture preview — declares it like any other sampled input and names its handle in the texture span:

```csharp
var map = g.Domain("map", 256, 256).Color("map.color", Format.Rgba8Srgb);
g.Pass("map").Reads(mapViewProj).Writes(map).Draw(ctx => DrawTopDown(ctx));
g.Pass("minimap").Samples(map).Blends(g.Backbuffer)        // .Samples orders it after "map" and makes it readable
    .Draw(panel, static (ctx, panel) => ctx.DrawList("ui", DrawListIdentity.Transient,
        panel.Textures,                                    // TextureRef[]: [whiteTexel, map]
        panel.Vertices, panel.Indices, panel.Commands, panel.Push));
```

### UI bridges

The UI libraries reach the GPU only through `DrawList`; each bridge is a stable producer a pass holds as state.

| Type (`namespace`) | Role |
|---|---|
| `UIPainter` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.Vysara`) | `UIPainter.Create(engine, host)` registers the `ui` technique and returns the painter for a Vysara `UIHost`. Call `Prepare()` once per frame after the host composites and before `engine.Render`: it uploads the images the frame's slot tables newly name, writes the new pixels of a source whose pixels changed into its texture in place (`IEngine.UpdateTexture`) and releases one nothing references any more (after the frames in flight, through `IEngine.ReleaseTexture`). `Draw(ctx, surface)` inside a pass only binds and submits, as many times in the frame as it likes, and throws if `Prepare` did not run before the frame. `SetExternalTexture(tag, ITextureHandle)` binds a graph texture to every Vysara `HostImageSource` with that tag; the UI pass declares it with `.Samples`, and a tag with no texture, or a colour space its format does not decode, fails `Prepare`. A source uploads as `Rgba8Srgb` or `Rgba8Unorm` by its colour space, and a straight-alpha one is premultiplied after filtering, as Vysara's rasterizer does. Textures the host reports released (`UIHost.ReleasedTextures`) are released in `Prepare`; a `WriteableBitmap`'s texture is updated in place on each `Invalidate`. |
| `VysaraInputLayer` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.Vysara`) | The input half: an `IInputLayer` that queues a frame's pointer, key and text events into a `UIHost` and blocks the layers below from what the host reported it wants. `PadNavigation`, while the app sets it (a menu or page a pad can work is open), turns any pad's face buttons into Vysara's `GamepadA`/`B`/`X`/`Y` and its d-pad and left stick into the d-pad's keys, a held direction repeating after 0.4 s every 0.09 s, and blocks the pad from the layers below: Vysara moves focus by position on the d-pad, and `GamepadA` presses a button. A touch that comes down on UI content (`UIHost.HitsContent`) is the UI's until it lifts, sent as a touch pointer and kept from the layers below; any other is theirs for its life, so a finger on a button and another on the game work at once. The block on what the host wants covers the mouse (and a pen's moves), never a touch. |
| `InWorldPanel` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.Vysara`) | A Vysara surface rendered into its own texture and placed in the world: `Create(engine, width, height, worldTransform, billboard, layoutScale)`, then per frame `QueueScreenPointer`, `Tick`, `Render` (composite + prepare) and `Draw(ctx)` in the pass that renders the panel's target. |
| `ImGuiPainter` (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.ImGui`) | `ImGuiPainter.Create(engine)` registers the `imgui` technique and uploads the font atlas; `Draw(ctx)` submits the frame's Dear ImGui draw data, plus the resource viewer's thumbnails (`SetThumbnails`, through `ResolveInspectable`) and debug lines (`SetDebugLines`). Desktop only. |

## World-anchored UI (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.Vysara`)

Screen-space Vysara elements that follow points in the world — labels over objects, markers along a path. App-side: the engine names no anchor; this sits in the Vysara bridge on top of `TryProjectToScreen`.

| Member | Role |
|---|---|
| `ScreenAnchors.Create(engine, view)` | Anchors that fill `view`, a `UIView` of their own (its root must be empty), reading `engine.ClipSpaceCorrection` once. Draw `anchors.View.Surface` with a `UIPainter` like any view. |
| `anchors.Add(element, world, alignment, pixelOffset)` → `ScreenAnchorId` | Wrap `element` in a container pinned to `world`: `alignment` is the fraction of the element's size that sits on the point ((0.5, 1) the middle of its bottom edge), `pixelOffset` a further offset in layout units. |
| `anchors.SetWorldPosition(id, world)` / `SetPlacement(id, alignment, pixelOffset)` / `Remove(id)` / `GetFade(id)` | Move, re-place, remove (a removed id throws if used again) and read an anchor's fade. |
| `anchors.Update(viewProjection, framebufferSize, deltaSeconds)` | Each frame between the host's `Tick` and `Render`: move every container to its projected point through `UIElement.Translation` (no layout) and step its fade — out while the point is off the viewport (beyond `ViewportMargin`) or behind the eye, on the container, so the element's own opacity is untouched. Allocates nothing. `FadeSeconds` sets the fade's length. |

---

# Kaldra's Pillars of Design

These are the load-bearing rules behind Kaldra's design. Each is easy to break without a compiler error and hard to notice once broken — violate one and the design quietly stops working. Hold them when adding or changing anything in the engine.

## Derived, not declared

Users state reads and writes only. The engine derives:

- **Execution order** — topological sort from the read/write edges.
- **Barriers and layout transitions** — from who last wrote and who next reads.
- **Transient-resource aliasing** — from lifetime analysis (non-overlapping lifetimes share memory).
- **CPU↔GPU sync** — from frame-in-flight tracking.

Any API that asks the user to specify *order* is a smell. If you find yourself wanting to place a barrier or sequence two passes by hand, express the dependency through a resource access instead and let the derivation do it.

## `.Writes` vs `.Blends`

`.Writes(handle)` means **produce**: the engine may clear the target before the pass runs. Use it when the pass is the sole writer of that resource this frame.

`.Blends(handle)` means **accumulate onto existing contents**: the engine preserves what's there (`LoadOp.Load`) and the technique's blend state layers on top. The pass is simultaneously the last reader and the next writer. Use it for multi-light forward passes, particle accumulation, and any "layer on top of" pattern.

The barrier derivation depends on the distinction. Getting them swapped produces wrong pixels, not a runtime error.

## Backend isolation / portability

All procedural, struct-heavy, graphics-API code lives in the backends (`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.Vulkan`, `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.DirectX12`). `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core` and `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph` carry no Vulkan or D3D12 type.

The dependency direction enforces it: `Sandbox → Backend → Graph → Core`. A reference the other way (Core → Backend) is the cardinal violation — it breaks portability and blocks a new backend from joining. Kaldra runs on Vulkan and DirectX 12 in parallel at pixel parity today, with Metal and WebGPU under investigation; that future depends on this isolation staying clean, so every new GPU feature must land in (or be capability-gated for) every backend.

## Pure per-frame closures

The graph is built once with `RenderGraph.Define` and cached; each `.Draw`/`.Dispatch` body then runs every frame. So a closure may capture **stable objects** — engine handles and app-side stable producers (a painter, a scene) — and read their **live** members at execute time; it must **not** capture a per-frame **value**, because that snapshot freezes at build time and never updates. Pull per-frame facts from `ctx` and per-frame data from neutral `Constants`/`Storage` buffers (`IEngine.Write(handle, …)`), or from a stable producer passed in as pass state.

**Correct** — pull a per-frame matrix from a constants channel the pass reads:

```csharp
var viewProj = g.Constants<Matrix4x4>("camera.viewproj");
g.Pass("gbuffer")
    .Reads(viewProj)
    .Writes(albedo)
    .Draw(static ctx => ctx.Draw(DrawCall.Create(mesh, "gbuffer")));
// each frame, before Render: engine.Write(viewProj, camera.ViewProjection);
```

**Incorrect** — capturing a value at definition time freezes it:

```csharp
var camera = GetCamera();          // stale every frame after the first
g.Pass("gbuffer").Writes(albedo)
    .Draw(ctx => DrawWith(ctx, camera));   // don't capture per-frame data
```

**Correct** — a stable producer (not a per-frame value) passed as pass state, so the body can be `static`:

```csharp
g.Pass("gbuffer").Writes(albedo)
    .Draw(scene, static (ctx, scene) => DrawWith(ctx, scene));   // scene.Camera read live, not snapshotted
```

A stable handle bundle created once for the engine's lifetime (a painter, a mesh store) is fine to capture directly — it isn't per-frame data. The `Draw<TState>`/`Dispatch<TState>` overloads exist for the cases where that stable state isn't already in scope: pass it explicitly and write the body `static`, so the compiler rejects any accidental capture of a per-frame value.

## No allocations on the hot path

The steady per-frame render loop allocates no managed memory (especially in Release). The graph is built once and cached; per-frame work runs through preallocated/pooled buffers, `ref struct`s, and spans. Scratch that grows on demand grows geometrically and then stays put, so steady state settles to zero allocations. This applies equally to Vysara's per-frame tick/route/composite path.

A `foreach` over an interface, a LINQ chain, a closure capture, or a boxed struct inside `.Draw` / `.Dispatch` / the compositor is a regression — reach for an indexed `for`, a pooled array, or a value type.

## The engine names no game concepts

There is no `Camera`, `Sun`, `Scene`, or `Cascade` in `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core` or `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph`. View, light, and time data ride in through neutral channels — the `Constants` and `Storage` buffers a pass reads, and the `FrameInputs` the app fills — and the app names its own views with its own keys. `Camera`, `Frustum`, and `Scene` exist only as app-side helpers in `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Concepts`: convenience, not engine vocabulary.

When a feature seems to need a named game concept in the engine, generalise it into a neutral channel the app fills instead.

## Ping-pong via handle swap

Iterative effects (bloom, the Jump Flood Algorithm) need two physical resources alternating between read and write. The pattern: allocate two handles, keep a `(read, write)` pair, swap them each iteration. The graph follows the handles — there is no special "ping-pong" concept in the engine.

```csharp
var (read, write) = (g.Screen.Color("jfa-a", Format.Rg16F), g.Screen.Color("jfa-b", Format.Rg16F));
for (var i = 0; i < iterations; i++)
{
    g.Pass($"jfa-{i}").Samples(read).Writes(write).Draw(ctx => …);
    (read, write) = (write, read);   // swap; the next pass reads what this one wrote
}
```

## Fail loud, never silently degrade

A backend mapping switch throws on a value it doesn't map rather than guessing. An API that over-promises throws at derive time rather than quietly doing the wrong thing. A device missing a required feature is rejected at engine creation, not worked around. The design would rather stop with a clear error than ship a subtly wrong frame.

---

## Other load-bearing properties

Not pillars, but engine guarantees worth knowing when working on the backends or the schedule:

- **Structural changes are cheap and cached.** `RenderGraph` is immutable and hashable, and `RenderGraph.Hash()` covers everything the Execute layer derives from — resources (including their clear attributes), passes, access edges, the present and readback targets — so equal hashes mean equal derived plans and equal GPU resource needs. `IEngine.SetGraph` with a structurally identical graph therefore skips the whole GPU half: no drain, no reallocation, and no loss of what those resources hold (`Persistent` history, written parameter buffers, pending readback). It still re-derives the schedule/barriers, because the plan carries *this* graph's `.Draw`/`.Dispatch` callbacks and reusing the previous graph's would silently render whatever the old closures captured; deriving is pure CPU work over immutable data, so it costs a fraction of the rebuild it replaces. A genuinely new graph rebakes, but the device and pipeline cache persist across swaps, so the new graph is warm from its first frame. It is therefore safe to call `RenderGraph.Define` every frame if the structure depends on runtime state: only structural changes (different passes, resources, or domains) trigger a rebake, while per-frame data travels via `FrameInputs` and `ctx`.
- **Vulkan baseline.** The Vulkan backend requires dynamic rendering, synchronization2, and timeline semaphores; barriers use `vkCmdPipelineBarrier2`, and there are no renderpass or framebuffer objects. A device without these features is rejected at engine creation (per *Fail loud* above).

---

# Getting Started with Kaldra

Kaldra is a declarative, render-graph-driven rendering engine for .NET 11, running on **Vulkan and DirectX 12 at pixel parity**. You declare *what* each pass reads and writes; the engine derives ordering, barriers, image-layout transitions, transient-memory aliasing, and CPU↔GPU synchronisation.

This guide takes you from an empty project to a two-pass render graph drawing a mesh to an offscreen HDR target and tone-mapping it to the screen. For the design rationale see [`docs/pillars.md`](pillars.md) and [`docs/architecture.md`](architecture.md); for the full feature list see [`README.md`](../README.md).

## Prerequisites

- .NET 11 SDK
- Windows (for DirectX 12 and signed DXIL compilation), or any platform (Vulkan only)
- Vulkan SDK 1.4+ with validation layers (recommended for development)

## Consumption mode 1: NuGet (recommended for new projects)

Add the SDK package to your `.csproj`:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Sdk" Version="0.1.0-preview.1" />
```

`BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Sdk` auto-injects the props and targets that pull in the backends. Select which backends to reference with MSBuild flags, set before the reference (or in `Directory.Build.props`):

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <UseVulkan>true</UseVulkan>
  <UseDirectX12>false</UseDirectX12>
  <!-- Optional UI integrations -->
  <UseVysara>false</UseVysara>
  <UseImGui>false</UseImGui>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Setting a flag to `true` adds the matching `PackageReference` automatically — you never reference `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.Vulkan` or `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.UI.Vysara` directly, and `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core` / `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Graph` / `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Assets` arrive transitively. `UseVysara` also brings Vysara's XAML generator: every `.xaml` view in the project compiles into its partial `x:Class`, XAML errors fail the build at the view's file and line, and `dotnet watch` hot-reloads an edited view. To compile your app's Slang shaders at build time, add:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <KaldraShaderSourceDir>$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)\Shaders</KaldraShaderSourceDir>
  <KaldraShaderOutputMode>Content</KaldraShaderOutputMode>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Slang sources in `Shaders/` compile to `.spv` / `.dxil` / `.json` under `shaders/` in your output, beside the executable — exactly where the backends resolve a technique's logical shader name.

## Consumption mode 2: Git submodule (for contributors or engine modifications)

```bash
git submodule add https://github.com/AtomicBlom/Kaldra external/Kaldra
git submodule update --init --recursive
```

Consume the SDK by writing the two import lines yourself:

```xml
<Import Project="external/Kaldra/build/BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Sdk/Sdk/Sdk.props" />

<PropertyGroup>
  <UseVulkan>true</UseVulkan>
  <KaldraShaderSourceDir>$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)\Shaders</KaldraShaderSourceDir>
  <KaldraShaderOutputMode>Content</KaldraShaderOutputMode>
</PropertyGroup>

<!-- … project body … -->

<Import Project="external/Kaldra/build/BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Sdk/Sdk/Sdk.targets" />
```

The submodule model gives you full engine source and the ability to modify the engine alongside your game. Both modes are first-class; there is no functional difference at runtime.

## Creating an engine

A backend is the factory for an `IEngine`. Each referenced backend assembly self-registers an `IRenderBackend` into `Backends.Available` as it loads, so the host discovers what is available at runtime and selects one by name. **Constructing a backend's settings subclass (`VulkanEngineSettings` / `DirectX12EngineSettings`) is what loads that backend's assembly** and fires its registration — it is the one sanctioned place a backend type appears in app code.

The host hands the backend the window's native surface *opaquely* — Kaldra names no windowing type. For Vulkan that is the window's `IVkSurface`; for DirectX 12 it is the window's `HWND`. Using Silk.NET for windowing:

```csharp
using BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Hosting;
using BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.Vulkan;

// A Vulkan-capable window (Silk.NET).
var options = WindowOptions.DefaultVulkan with { Size = new Vector2D<int>(1280, 720), Title = "My Kaldra app" };
var window = Window.Create(options);
window.Initialize();

if (window.VkSurface is null)
    throw new InvalidOperationException("The windowing platform did not expose a Vulkan surface.");

// Constructing VulkanEngineSettings loads BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.Vulkan, which registers the backend.
var settings = new VulkanEngineSettings
{
    EnableValidation = true,        // Vulkan validation layers (dev)
    VSync           = true,
    HdrOutput       = false,
    PreferredBackend = "Vulkan",
};

// Select the backend by name and create the engine bound to the surface.
var backend = Backends.Available.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Name == settings.PreferredBackend)
              ?? Backends.Available.First();
using var engine = backend.Create(window.VkSurface, window.FramebufferSize.X, window.FramebufferSize.Y, settings);
```

For DirectX 12, create a context-less window (`API = GraphicsAPI.None`), construct `DirectX12EngineSettings` (which loads `BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.DirectX12`), and pass the window's `HWND` as the surface:

```csharp
using BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Backend.DirectX12;

var settings = new DirectX12EngineSettings
{
    EnableValidation = true,        // D3D12 debug layer (dev)
    PreferredBackend = "DirectX12",
};

var hwnd = window.Native?.Win32?.Hwnd
           ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("The DirectX12 backend needs the window's Win32 HWND.");

var backend = Backends.Available.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Name == settings.PreferredBackend)
              ?? Backends.Available.First();
using var engine = backend.Create(hwnd, window.FramebufferSize.X, window.FramebufferSize.Y, settings);
```

The neutral `EngineSettings` base carries `EnableValidation`, `VSync`, `MaxFramesPerSecond`, `HdrOutput`, `PreferredBackend`, and `WatchShaderDirectory` (dev shader hot-reload). Each subclass adds its own knobs (e.g. `PreferDiscreteGpu`, a `ShaderDirectory`). Call `engine.Resize(width, height)` when the window resizes, and dispose the engine (it drains the GPU first) on shutdown.

## Minimal example: two-pass render graph

This renders a mesh into an offscreen HDR buffer, then tone-maps that buffer to the swapchain. It shows the whole loop: shaders, techniques, a graph, and the per-frame call.

### 1. Define shaders

Author shaders in **Slang**; the SDK compiles them offline to SPIR-V (Vulkan), signed DXIL (DirectX 12), and WGSL (WebGPU), and the backend derives descriptor-binding layouts from the emitted reflection JSON — you never hand-count bindings, nor hand-order them. The technique descriptor's default entry points are `vertexMain` / `fragmentMain`, so name your stages to match.

Every shader starts by including the platform module, which owns the places the three targets disagree. [`shader-authoring.md`](shader-authoring.md) is the full contract; the two rules you need here are that resources take **no binding numbers or registers** (Slang numbers them per target, in declaration order, and each backend binds by its reflection), and that a shader writing clip space directly uses a `KALDRA_*_POS` macro rather than doing it by hand.

`Shaders/scene.slang` — a lit mesh. It reads the per-frame view-projection from a constants buffer the pass `.Reads`, and a per-draw model matrix from the per-draw uniform block:

```slang
#include "kaldra_platform.module.slang"

struct ViewProj { float4x4 viewProj; }   // filled from the app via engine.Write(viewProj, …)
struct PerDraw  { float4x4 model; }      // staged by DrawCall.SetUniforms(ref block)

// No numbers: Slang gives each target its own, in declaration order.
// Uniform slots fill in a defined order: the pass's .Reads constants first, then the per-draw block.
ConstantBuffer<ViewProj> view;
ConstantBuffer<PerDraw>  draw;

struct VSOut { float4 pos : SV_Position; float3 normal : NORMAL; }

[shader("vertex")]
VSOut vertexMain(float3 pos : POSITION, float3 normal : NORMAL)
{
    VSOut o;
    float4 world = mul(draw.model, float4(pos, 1.0));
    o.pos = mul(view.viewProj, world);
    o.normal = mul((float3x3)draw.model, normal);
    return o;
}

[shader("fragment")]
float4 fragmentMain(VSOut i) : SV_Target
{
    float light = saturate(dot(normalize(i.normal), normalize(float3(0.4, 0.8, 0.3))));
    return float4(float3(1.0, 0.6, 0.2) * (0.2 + 0.8 * light), 1.0);
}
```

`Shaders/tonemap.slang` — a fullscreen pass that samples the HDR target and maps it to display range. A fullscreen technique fabricates its own triangle, so it has no vertex input:

```slang
#include "kaldra_platform.module.slang"

Sampler2D hdr;   // the pass's first .Samples input

struct VSOut { float4 pos : SV_Position; float2 uv : TEXCOORD0; }

[shader("vertex")]
VSOut vertexMain(uint id : SV_VertexID)
{
    // Fullscreen triangle from the vertex id — no mesh. KALDRA_FULLSCREEN_POS applies the NDC-Y convention this
    // target needs; writing `uv * 2 - 1` by hand renders upside down on WebGPU.
    float2 uv = float2((id << 1) & 2, id & 2);
    VSOut o;
    o.pos = KALDRA_FULLSCREEN_POS(uv);
    o.uv = uv;
    return o;
}

[shader("fragment")]
float4 fragmentMain(VSOut i) : SV_Target
{
    float3 c = hdr.Sample(i.uv).rgb;
    c = c / (c + 1.0);                       // Reinhard tone-map
    return float4(c, 1.0);
}
```

### 2. Register techniques

A technique names its shader *logically* and states its pipeline intent. `HasVertexInput: true` means the technique reads a mesh's vertex stream; left default, the technique fabricates a fullscreen triangle (the tone-map). Register both up front, before the graph draws with them:

```csharp
using BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Materials;

engine.DefineTechnique("scene", new TechniqueDescriptor("scene", HasVertexInput: true));
engine.DefineTechnique("tonemap", new TechniqueDescriptor("tonemap"));
```

### 3. Define the render graph

A graph is built once with `RenderGraph.Define` and set on the engine with `SetGraph`. You declare each pass's reads and writes — never the order or the barriers — and `g.Present` names the target shown on screen. Per-frame view data rides a neutral `Constants` channel the scene pass reads; the engine names no camera.

The graph is immutable and cached by hash, so re-setting a structurally identical one is cheap: the engine reuses the GPU resources it already built (and everything they hold — cross-frame `Persistent` history, your written parameter buffers) and only re-derives the plan. You can rebuild and set the graph whenever the structure *might* have changed rather than tracking that by hand; only a real structural change pays for a rebuild.

```csharp
using System.Numerics;
using BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Graph;
using BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Core.Hosting;

var graph = RenderGraph.Define(g =>
{
    // Offscreen HDR colour + depth, both at native screen resolution.
    var hdr   = g.Screen.Color("hdr",   Format.Rgba16F);
    var depth = g.Screen.Depth("depth", Format.Depth32F);

    // A per-frame uniform channel the scene pass reads (filled each frame via engine.Write).
    var viewProj = g.Constants<Matrix4x4>("camera.viewproj");

    // Scene pass: read the view-projection, write HDR colour + depth. The body only needs `scene` — a
    // stable producer, not a per-frame value — so pass it as pass state via the Draw<TState> overload:
    // a `static` lambda can then reach only `scene` and `ctx`, so a per-frame value can't accidentally
    // be captured and frozen at build time.
    g.Pass("scene")
        .Reads(viewProj)
        .Writes(hdr)
        .WritesDepth(depth)
        .Draw(scene, static (ctx, scene) =>
        {
            // Your own draw list, however you build it — scene.VisibleObjects is read live each frame.
            foreach (var obj in scene.VisibleObjects)
            {
                var call = DrawCall.Create(obj.Mesh, "scene");
                call.Material = obj.Material;          // fills the technique's reflected sampler slots
                // The per-draw block matching the shader. `ref` because the bytes alias this storage until the
                // draw is submitted — passing a temporary would leave the engine reading a dead local, so the
                // compiler rejects it rather than letting it corrupt at runtime.
                var model = obj.ModelMatrix;
                call.SetUniforms(ref model);
                ctx.Draw(call);
            }
        });

    // Tonemap pass: sample HDR, write the swapchain. `hdr` is a build-time resource handle (not
    // per-frame data), so capturing it directly is fine — only per-frame values need the state overload.
    g.Pass("tonemap")
        .Samples(hdr)
        .Writes(g.Backbuffer)
        .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("tonemap", hdr));

    // The terminal: present the swapchain. Acquire/present sync is derived behind this.
    g.Present(g.Backbuffer);
});

engine.SetGraph(graph);
```

The pass-builder verbs are the whole scheduling vocabulary — `.Writes` (produce a colour target), `.Blends` (accumulate onto existing contents), `.Samples` (bind as a shader-read input), `.WritesDepth` / `.ReadsDepth`, `.ReadWrites` (compute storage), `.ReadsVertex` (a vertex/instance stream), and `.Reads` (a constants or storage buffer). From these the engine derives execution order, every barrier, and every layout transition.

### 4. Render loop

`FrameInputs` carries only `DeltaSeconds` and `Time` (both `double`) — there is no engine `Camera` or `Scene`. View, light, and time data flow in through the neutral channels your passes read: write them by handle each frame *before* `Render`. Driven by Silk.NET's render callback:

```csharp
var elapsed = 0.0;   // double: an accumulator kept as float loses precision over a long session

window.Render += delta =>
{
    elapsed += delta;

    // Publish the matrix the "scene" pass reads. (BinaryVibrance.Kaldra.Concepts.Camera folds in the
    // clip-space correction so the same matrix is correct on both backends.)
    engine.Write(viewProj, camera.ViewProjection);
```
